section_headings: 2.1.3. Sustained VT and VF Not Associated With ACS
content.narrative_summary: Section 2.1.3 describes sustained ventricular tachycardia (VT) and ventricular fibrillation (VF) not related to acute coronary syndrome, noting their mechanisms, risk factors in structural and idiopathic contexts, and associations with channelopathies and long QT syndrome. Section 2.2 reviews sudden cardiac death (SCD), with 2.2.1 detailing its incidence and public health burden in the United States, including out-of-hospital and in-hospital arrest rates and survival statistics. Section 2.2.2 discusses challenges in population and individual risk prediction for sudden cardiac arrest, highlights epidemiological markers, age-related risk stratification, subgroup identification, and lifetime risk patterns.

The page discusses that ischemic heart disease remains the most common substrate for sudden cardiac death (SCD) but its incidence is decreasing, while cardiomyopathies with fibrosis and hypertrophy are increasing. It notes a trend toward more high-risk profiles among out-of-hospital cardiac arrest survivors and highlights that younger patients (children through young adults) are affected by genetic structural disorders, channelopathies, myocarditis, congenital heart disease, and other rare conditions. It emphasizes the challenge of identifying small high-risk subgroups within the general population who may experience SCD as a first event. The text introduces mechanisms of ventricular arrhythmias (VA), including enhanced and abnormal automaticity, triggered activity (early or late afterdepolarizations), and reentry, with triggers such as premature ventricular complexes and substrates like structural scars.

3. In patients with suspected or documented VA, a 12-lead ECG should be obtained in sinus rhythm to look for evidence of heart disease (S4.2.1-6).

section_headings: 5. Therapies for Treatment or Prevention of VA
content.narrative_summary: The synopsis outlines the role of electrophysiological study (EPS) to induce sustained ventricular arrhythmias in patients with known or suspected VA, noting fewer indications since ICD benefit is established. It discusses EPS to guide ablation, diagnose wide complex tachycardias or SVT, and highlights limited prognostic value in channelopathies. Recommendation‐specific supportive text presents evidence that inducible VT/VF in ischemic cardiomyopathy and NICM correlates with outcomes, whereas routine EPS solely for risk stratification in ICD‐eligible patients lacks support.

rows.recommendation: In patients with ischemic cardiomyopathy, NICM, or adult congenital heart disease who have syncope or other VA symptoms and who do not meet indications for a primary prevention ICD, an electrophysiological study can be useful for assessing the risk of sustained VT (S4.3.2-1—S4.3.2-7).
In patients who meet criteria for ICD implantation, an electrophysiological study for the sole reason of inducing VA is not indicated for risk stratification (S4.3.2-8—S4.3.2-11).

An electrophysiological study is not recommended for risk stratification for VA in the setting of long QT syndrome, catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia, short QT syndrome, or early repolarization syndromes (S4.3.2-12—S4.3.2-16).

It then reviews the efficacy and safety of beta blockers in ventricular arrhythmia management and SCD risk reduction in various patient populations (HF, post-MI, polymorphic VT), and introduces amiodarone and sotalol’s multichannel blockade properties and the controversy over their long-term survival benefits.

content.narrative_summary: The page continues discussion of statin trials showing reduced SCD risk in patients with or at risk for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, noting that benefits are not seen in heart failure populations without ischemia. Section 5.2 introduces pharmacologic prevention of SCD in HFrEF, highlighting that beta blockers, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, and renin–angiotensin system inhibitors reduce arrhythmogenic mechanisms, ventricular remodeling, and mortality. Randomized trials of bisoprolol, carvedilol, metoprolol, and sacubitril/valsartan consistently demonstrate reductions in all-cause mortality, VA, and SCD. Section 5.3 begins discussion of ICDs and defibrillators for treatment of ventricular arrhythmias and SCD.

5.5. Surgery and Revascularization Procedures in Patients With Ischemic Heart Disease
content.narrative_summary: This page discusses catheter ablation for ventricular arrhythmias. It outlines general considerations for ablation in ventricular arrhythmia when antiarrhythmic medications are ineffective or not tolerated, including approaches to mapping and access (transvenous, transaortic, epicardial) and limitations when arrhythmia cannot be induced or originates in inaccessible regions. It then addresses ablation in idiopathic VA in patients without structural heart disease, emphasizing focal mapping and endocardial catheterization. Finally, it describes scar-related VT in structural heart disease, highlighting identification and elimination of surviving myocardial channels in fibrous scar and the advanced mapping and multidisciplinary support required.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Surgery and Revascularization Procedures in Patients With Ischemic Heart Disease

rows.recommendation: 1. Patients with sustained VA and survivors of SCA should be evaluated for ischemic heart disease, and should be revascularized as appropriate (S5.5-1—S5.5-4).
2. In patients with anomalous origin of a coronary artery suspected to be the cause of SCA, repair or revascularization is recommended.

section_headings: Recommendations for Management of Cardiac Arrest
content.narrative_summary: The synopsis explains that sympathetic activation is proarrhythmic and parasympathetic activation antiarrhythmic. Autonomic modulation—by interrupting sympathetic outflow or stimulating the parasympathetic pathway—may prevent ventricular arrhythmias; it is effective in long QT syndrome and catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia but has limited broader data and no formal recommendation (S5.6-5). The recommendation-specific supportive text notes that many patients with non-life-threatening ventricular arrhythmias require only reassurance, though atenolol reduces arrhythmic burden in symptomatic VA (S5.6-1), and that cardiac sympathetic denervation can reduce arrhythmias and may be reasonable for refractory VT/VF storm despite limited data (S5.6-3, S5.6-4–5.6-6).

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Management of Cardiac Arrest

rows.recommendation: CPR should be performed in patients in cardiac arrest, according to published basic and advanced cardiovascular life support algorithms (S6-1–S6-3).

In patients with hemodynamically unstable VA that persist or recur after a maximal energy shock, intravenous amiodarone should be administered to attempt to achieve a stable rhythm after further defibrillation (S6-1,S6-4–S6-6).
Patients presenting with VA with hemodynamic instability should undergo direct current cardioversion (S6-1–S6-3).
In patients with polymorphic VT or VF with ST-elevation MI, angiography with emergency revascularization is recommended (S6-7–S6-10).
Patients with a wide-QRS tachycardia should be presumed to have VT if the diagnosis is unclear.
In patients with hemodynamically stable VT, administration of intravenous procainamide can be useful to attempt to terminate VT (S6-11–S6-13).

In patients with a witnessed cardiac arrest due to VF or polymorphic VT that is unresponsive to CPR, defibrillation, and vasopressor therapy, intravenous lidocaine can be beneficial (S6-1,S6-4,S6-5,S6-14,S6-15).
In patients with polymorphic VT due to myocardial ischemia, intravenous beta blockers can be useful (S6-16,S6-17).

content.narrative_summary: This section describes the low incidence but high mortality of sustained VT/VF after CABG, including early postoperative VF due to reperfusion and metabolic disturbances. It differentiates polymorphic VT/VF associated with ischemia from monomorphic VT linked to old infarcts and scars, highlighting the need for myocardial ischemia treatment, graft patency evaluation, and management of mechanical or electrolyte complications. Risk factors for monomorphic VT early after CABG include prior MI, ventricular scar, LV dysfunction, and bypass graft placement. Symptomatic ventricular arrhythmias post-CABG should follow existing acute and ongoing VT management recommendations; ICD implantation did not improve survival in patients without sustained VT/VF but LV dysfunction. For those undergoing revascularization, reassessment of LV function at 3 months may inform ICD decisions. High NSVT burden with reduced LVEF may warrant electrophysiological risk stratification, and inducible sustained VT patients may benefit from ICD. The wearable cardioverter-defibrillator may be used early after revascularization to allow ventricular recovery.

rows.recommendation: In patients with LVEF of 35% or less that is due to ischemic heart disease who are at least 40 days’ post-MI and at least 90 days postrevascularization, and with NYHA class II or III HF despite GDMT, an ICD is recommended if meaningful survival of greater than 1 year is expected (S7.1.2-1, S7.1.2-2).

In patients with LVEF of 30% or less that is due to ischemic heart disease who are at least 40 days’ post-MI and at least 90 days postrevascularization, and with NYHA class I HF despite GDMT, an ICD is recommended if meaningful survival of greater than 1 year is expected (S7.1.2-2, S7.1.2-3).

A transvenous ICD provides high value in the primary prevention of SCD particularly when the patient's risk of death due to a VA is deemed high and the risk of nonarrhythmic death (either cardiac or noncardiac) is deemed low based on the patient's burden of comorbidities and functional status (S7.1.2-4).

In patients with NSVT due to prior MI, LVEF of 40% or less and inducible sustained VT or VF at electrophysiological study, an ICD is recommended if meaningful survival of greater than 1 year is expected (S7.1.2-5).

In nonhospitalized patients with NYHA class IV symptoms who are candidates for cardiac transplantation or an LVAD, an ICD is reasonable if meaningful survival of greater than 1 year is expected (S7.1.2-6–S7.1.2-9).

An ICD is not indicated for NYHA class IV patients with medication-refractory HF who are not also candidates for cardiac transplantation, an LVAD, or a CRT defibrillator that incorporates both pacing and defibrillation capabilities.

content.narrative_summary: Arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy is an inherited disease predominantly affecting the right ventricle, with fibrofatty myocardial replacement leading to ventricular arrhythmias and sudden cardiac death. Clinical screening using ECG, imaging, ambulatory rhythm monitoring, and exercise testing identifies at‐risk first‐degree relatives. ARVC is often due to autosomal dominant desmosomal protein mutations with variable penetrance; approximately 35% of relatives test positive, with 8–16% experiencing major arrhythmic events over long‐term follow‐up. Genetic counseling and targeted testing guide family screening. Cardiac MRI provides high‐quality assessment of ventricular structure, function, scar, and fibrosis.

content.title: 7.9.1.2. Catecholaminergic Polymorphic Ventricular Tachycardia
section_headings: Recommendations for Catecholaminergic Polymorphic Ventricular Tachycardia
content.narrative_summary: The page provides supportive text for catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia (CPVT). It describes CPVT as characterized by exertion‐related bidirectional or polymorphic ventricular tachycardia associated with syncope and sudden cardiac arrest, occurring in 3%–13% of patients. Treatment with beta blockers reduces adverse cardiac events, and nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers may offer additional benefit. Flecainide combined with beta blockers can suppress ventricular ectopy by up to 76%, with verapamil or propafenone as alternatives. ICD implantation is reserved for those with prior sudden cardiac arrest or refractory ventricular arrhythmias, though inappropriate shock rates are 20%–30%, highlighting the need for optimized programming. Left cardiac sympathetic denervation decreases recurrent ICD shocks by 32%–75% and is best performed at experienced centers. Genetic testing assists in confirming diagnosis and screening first‐degree relatives; ryanodine receptor mutations are found in about 47% of probands and calmodulin mutations in young idiopathic VF patients, though genotype status does not reliably predict disease severity or medication response.

content.narrative_summary: The page continues a discussion of VA ablation complications and antiarrhythmic vs catheter ablation comparisons. For papillary muscle VA, the LV or RV papillary muscles can be the origin of PVCs and NSVT in the presence or absence of structural heart disease. Idiopathic papillary muscle VA is often exercise-related, induced by catecholamines, and treated effectively with catheter ablation despite challenges in catheter stability; recurrences are more frequent than with idiopathic outflow tract VA, but serious complications are rare. For interfascicular reentrant VT, reentry within the LV Purkinje system (often the left posterior fascicle) causes sustained VT with typical right bundle-branch block QRS morphology. Antiarrhythmic drug therapy is ineffective, and verapamil (intravenous for acute termination; chronic oral for recurrent cases) and catheter ablation are useful.

content.narrative_summary: The page begins with continuation of idiopathic VF discussion, then introduces PVC-induced cardiomyopathy. content.title: Subcutaneous Implantable Cardioverter-Defibrillator
content.narrative_summary: The Synopsis describes that preimplant ECG screening to establish QRS-T morphology is required to reduce undersensing of VT/VF and inappropriate shocks. The subcutaneous ICD is implanted using anatomical landmarks without fluoroscopy, consisting of a pulse generator at the midaxillary line and a subcutaneous lead adjacent to the sternum. It cannot provide bradycardia or antitachycardia pacing. Both transvenous and subcutaneous ICDs include SVT/VT discriminators, but subcutaneous devices deliver painful awake shocks and limited postshock pacing. Recommendation-Specific Supportive Text notes that the subcutaneous ICD avoids venous access and related complications (eg, pneumothorax, hemothorax, tamponade) but may face challenges in patients with limited venous access such as ESRD; in a study of 27 ESRD patients the device was not associated with an…

In patients who meet indication for an ICD, implantation of a subcutaneous implantable cardioverter-defibrillator is reasonable if pacing for bradycardia or VT termination or as part of CRT is neither needed nor anticipated (S11.1-1–S11.1-4).

content.title: 11.2 Wearable Cardioverter-Defibrillator
content.narrative_summary: The synopsis describes the wearable cardioverter-defibrillator as a vest-like device worn under clothing that continuously monitors heart rhythm and automatically delivers an electric shock when VF or VT is detected. The device is intended to be worn continuously, 24 hours per day, except when the wearer is bathing or showering. It has been approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration for patients who are at risk for sudden cardiac arrest and are not candidates for or refuse an implantable defibrillator. AHA science advisory data and recommendations support its use, and its effectiveness in the recognition and defibrillation of ventricular fibrillation has been demonstrated.

content.title: 16. COST AND VALUE CONSIDERATIONS
content.narrative_summary: This section discusses economic assessments of ICD therapy, emphasizing that value evaluations use empirical clinical trial and observational designs as well as simulation models to compare lifetime outcomes and costs. It notes that initial ICD device and implantation costs are high and largely fixed, with long-term cost savings being modest. Model-based cost-effectiveness estimates are preferred over limited trial follow-up data, applying ACC/AHA benchmarks for value ratings. The cost‐effectiveness ratio is highly sensitive to the extension of survival time, favoring ICD use when arrhythmic death risk is high relative to nonarrhythmic death risk. Empirical evidence suggests limited benefit of ICDs for primary prevention when implanted early after CABG or myocardial infarction. Patient selection based on risk factors (e.g., LVEF ≤35% vs >35%) influences cost-effectiveness, with greater benefit in higher-risk groups and minimal variation by age.

content.narrative_summary: The page begins mid-discussion of ICD effectiveness, noting that most studies have focused on patients with reduced LV function post-MI or NICM, with limited data on channelopathies or HCM and little evidence of value in low-risk patients.
